findings.source_passage: what depths of the soul does Jonah's deep sealine sound! what a pregnant lesson to us is this prophet! What a noble thing is that canticle in the fish's belly! How billow-like and boisterously grand! We feel the floods surging over us
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Shipmates, this book, containing only four chapters'
findings.why_it_matters: This rhetorical cascade—'deep sealine,' 'canticle in the fish's belly,' 'billow-like and boisterously grand'—is prosodically and rhetorically distinctive Melville, establishing the sermon's maritime-theological register; the draft collapses it to 'what depths it sounds!'
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full rhetorical question chain verbatim: 'what depths of the soul does Jonah's deep sealine sound! what a pregnant lesson…billow-like and boisterously grand! We feel the floods surging over us.'

findings.source_passage: 'Who's there?' cries the Captain at his busy desk... Oh! how that harmless question mangles Jonah! For the instant he almost turns to flee again.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning "'Who's there?' cries the Captain"
findings.why_it_matters: The entire dramatized Captain-Jonah cabin dialogue—including the interpretively pivotal 'how that harmless question mangles Jonah'—is cut; this scene is critical to the sermon's psychological portrait of guilt and bears significant critical attention.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the cabin dialogue, at minimum the line ''Who's there?' Oh! how that harmless question mangles Jonah!' and the exchange about passage money / 'Soon enough for any honest man.'

findings.source_passage: Now Jonah's Captain, shipmates, was one whose discernment detects crime in any, but whose cupidity exposes it only in the penniless.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Now Jonah's Captain, shipmates, was one'
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of Melville's most sharply ironic social-critical sentences in the entire sermon; the draft replaces it with only the generalized 'sin that pays its way' maxim, losing the specific accusatory wit against corrupt authority.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: 'Jonah's Captain…was one whose discernment detects crime in any, but whose cupidity exposes it only in the penniless' before or alongside the 'sin that pays its way' passage.

findings.source_passage: so disordered, self-condemning is his look, that had there been policemen in those days, Jonah, on the mere suspicion of something wrong, had been arrested ere he touched a deck
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'With this sin of disobedience in him'
findings.why_it_matters: This anachronistic 'policemen' jest is distinctively Melvillean comic irony and is widely noted by critics as characteristic of the sermon's satirical voice; its absence is a voice erasure.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the policemen sentence after the 'vile burglar' passage.

findings.source_passage: Is not the main-truck higher than the kelson is low? Delight is to him—a far, far upward, and inward delight—who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth
findings.why_it_matters: 'Is not the main-truck higher than the kelson is low?' is a famous, widely quoted line anchoring the sermon's culminating rhetoric; its absence removes the structural pivot of the entire delight passage.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'Is not the main-truck higher than the kelson is low?' immediately before the delight anaphora.

findings.source_passage: whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the boisterous mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages.
findings.why_it_matters: 'The sure Keel of the Ages' is one of the sermon's most recognizable phrases, frequently anthologized; it is entirely absent from the draft's delight anaphora.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the fifth delight clause verbatim: 'Delight is to him, whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the boisterous mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages.'

findings.source_passage: prowling among the shipping like a vile burglar hastening to cross the seas. So disordered, self-condemning is his look
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'With this sin of disobedience in him'
findings.why_it_matters: The vivid 'vile burglar' simile and the full self-condemning portrait are truncated to 'guilty eye,' losing the rhetorical energy of the preacher's vivid narrative dramatization.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'skulking from his God; prowling among the shipping like a vile burglar hastening to cross the seas' after 'slouched hat and guilty eye.'

findings.source_passage: Another runs to read the bill that's stuck against the spile upon the wharf…offering five hundred gold coins for the apprehension of a parricide
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'With this sin of disobedience in him,' mid-section on mariners
findings.why_it_matters: The parricide bill detail is a vivid, specific comic-dramatic moment in the sermon's retelling that characterizes Mapple's narrative art; its omission flattens the scene to a summary.
findings.suggested_fix: Add at least one sentence restoring the bill-reading sailors and the parricide detail as part of the mariners' suspicion scene.

findings.source_passage: but all the things that God would have us do are hard for us to do—remember that—and hence, he oftener commands us than endeavors to persuade. And if we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it is in this disobeying ourselves, wherein the hardness of obeying God consists.
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves only the 'disobey ourselves' clause and omits 'he oftener commands us than endeavors to persuade' and the concluding restatement; the full formulation is a theologically weighted and rhetorically balanced signature statement.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'hence, he oftener commands us than endeavors to persuade. And if we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it is in this disobeying ourselves, wherein the hardness of obeying God consists.'

findings.source_passage: a panther billow leaping over the bulwarks. Wave after wave thus leaps into the ship…the white moon shows her affrighted face from the steep gullies in the blackness overhead
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'And now the time of tide has come'
findings.why_it_matters: The storm-at-sea imagery—'panther billow,' 'white moon shows her affrighted face,' rearing bowsprit—is some of Melville's most vivid prose in the sermon; the draft skips from Jonah sleeping to the lot-casting without any of this.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum the 'panther billow' and the moon/bowsprit images to preserve the storm's narrative and atmospheric intensity.

summary: The draft preserves the hymn and the Woe/Delight anaphoras adequately but loses multiple high-severity signatures: the sealine rhetorical cascade, the entire Captain cabin dialogue including 'how that harmless question mangles Jonah,' the social-critical cupidity sentence, the policemen jest, 'the main-truck higher than the kelson,' and 'the sure Keel of the Ages'—collectively constituting severe voice erasure and signature loss requiring regeneration.
